Emphasize the performance impact of the general query log and the importance of log rotation and monitoring. Include a security tip on how to detect brute-force attacks from the error log.

screens.title: Auditing and Logging for Security
screens.narratorSegment: Logs are the backbone of database security monitoring. In this lesson you will learn how the MySQL error log, general query log, slow query log, and binary log each provide distinct signals that help you detect failed logins, track suspicious queries, and reconstruct data changes. You will also see when and how to use the MySQL Enterprise Audit Log for compliance-grade, tamper-resistant event tracking. Practical configuration examples show where to set file paths and how to enable logs temporarily for forensic work. We will cover rotation and retention so logs do not exhaust disk space, plus simple monitoring tactics to alert on brute-force attempts, privilege changes, and unusual data-modifying activity. By the end, you will understand how to choose which logs to enable in production, how to collect them safely, and how logs fit into incident response workflows. Think about a time you needed to answer who changed a table and when; the techniques here explain which log will help you and how to preserve that evidence.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Auditing and Logging for Security
Auditing and Logging for Security
Use MySQL logs to detect incidents, support forensics, and meet compliance needs.
In this lesson
Configure logs, run temporary forensic captures, rotate and retain logs, and monitor for suspicious events.
Why it matters
Logs let you detect brute-force attempts, find unauthorized data changes, and produce evidence for audits.
Explore Key Topics
Log Types
Error, general, slow, and binary logs—each supplies a different security signal.
Rotation & Retention
Automate rotation to conserve disk and preserve critical audit history for compliance.
Monitoring
Parse logs and alert on repeated failures, privilege changes, and large data modifications.
Concept Map
Logs & Roles
Error log for server issues and failed logins; general query log for forensic sessions; slow query log for resource-abuse signals; binary log for immutable change history.
This presentation follows a terminal and command-focused style for practical demonstrations and config walk-throughs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will identify and configure the MySQL logs that matter for security, explain how each log supports incident response, and implement basic log management strategies. First, you will learn to find and set the error, general, slow, and binary log file paths and enable them when appropriate. Second, you will know how to use logs during an investigation — for example, enabling the general query log temporarily to capture forensic detail, or using the binary log to reconstruct data-modifying statements. Third, you will understand the benefits of the MySQL Enterprise Audit Log for compliance and how it differs from standard logs. Finally, you will implement rotation and retention rules and design simple monitoring rules to alert on repeated failures or anomalous changes. Each objective includes a practical competency milestone so you can verify your setup and test a scenario. These objectives focus on secure, evidence-preserving logging rather than indiscriminate verbosity.

screens.title: Why MySQL Logs are Security Sensors
screens.narratorSegment: Think of MySQL logs as complementary security sensors. The error log reveals server-level errors and authentication failures; the slow query log surfaces resource-heavy statements that could indicate abuse; the general query log is a complete but noisy record of client activity useful for short forensic captures; and the binary log provides an immutable record of data changes. Together these logs help you detect attack patterns — repeated failed logins in the error log, sudden schema changes recorded in the binary log, or a flurry of data-modifying statements that might indicate exfiltration. A common misconception is to enable every log permanently. That increases disk usage and can hurt performance, and it creates so much noise that meaningful alerts can be lost. Instead, treat logs as a layered strategy: enable essential, low-cost logs like the error log and binary log in production, use slow logs where resource abuse is a concern, and enable the general query log only temporarily during an investigation. The practical takeaway is to design logging that preserves evidence without overwhelming your system or analysts. Why MySQL Logs are Security Sensors means choose logs by their signal and cost: error and binary logs for continuous coverage; slow logs for resource monitoring; general log only for targeted forensic capture.. In practical terms, understanding the unique signal each log provides. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Why MySQL Logs are Security Sensors
Definition
Logs as security signals
Each log focuses on a different class of events. Choosing which to enable depends on the kind of evidence you need and the production cost you can accept.
Error log
Server errors, failed logins, SSL issues, crashes — low overhead and always useful.
Binary log
All data-modifying statements for replication and forensic reconstruction.
Slow query log
Queries exceeding a threshold; flags resource abuse or exfiltration attempts.
General query log
Every statement and connection; extremely verbose — useful only temporarily for forensics.
Examples & Guidance
Concrete examples that show when to rely on each log and a common mistake to avoid.
Example: Failed logins
Repeated failed authentication attempts will appear in the error log and should trigger an alert for possible brute-force.
Example: Data tampering
To determine which statements modified a table, consult the binary log or a temporarily enabled general log for precise query text.
Key takeaway
Design logging by cost and value: continuous low-cost logs plus temporary, high-detail captures when needed.

screens.title: Error Log: The First Line of Defense
screens.narratorSegment: The error log is the foundational MySQL log for security. It records server startup and shutdown events, warnings, non-fatal errors, fatal errors, and importantly, authentication failures and access denied messages. For security monitoring you use the error log to spot repeated failed logins that may indicate brute-force attempts and to find SSL loading errors which can weaken encrypted connections. The error log path is configured via the log_error variable in my. cnf; a typical setting points to /var/log/mysql/error. log. Regularly review the error log and ensure it is writable only by privileged users to preserve integrity. A common misconception is to treat the error log as proof of every attack; it can miss successful but stealthy data modifications. So use the error log as an early-warning sensor that should feed alerts for further investigation, not as a sole source of truth. Your next steps are to confirm log_error is set and to build alerts for repeated authentication failures. Error Log: The First Line of Defense means use the error log to detect server-level issues and authentication problems; configure secure file paths and alert on repeated failures.. In practical terms, detect server issues, failed logins, and ssl problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Error Log
Core Concept
Error Log
Records startup, shutdown, warnings, crashes, and authentication errors that are vital for security monitoring.
Config example
log_error=/var/log/mysql/error.log in my.cnf directs error output to a secure file path.
Security signals
Failed login bursts, access denied errors, and SSL loading problems should generate alerts and prompt investigation.
Common mistake
Ignoring permissions on the log file. Ensure only privileged accounts can read or alter logs to preserve evidence.
Example scenario
If the error log shows many 'Access denied' lines from the same client IP, treat that as a potential brute-force attack and block or rate-limit the source while you investigate.
Key takeaway
Keep the error log enabled in production and feed its alerts into your monitoring stack as an early-warning sensor.

screens.title: General Query Log: Forensics with Cost
screens.narratorSegment: The general query log records every statement a client executes along with connection and disconnection events. It is the most detailed trace you can get from MySQL, which makes it extremely valuable for forensic analysis when you need to see exactly what queries a compromised account executed. However, it comes at a heavy cost: high disk usage and significant performance overhead if left on in production. The recommended approach is to enable the general query log only temporarily for debugging or incident response, capture the activity you need, then disable it. For runtime control, you can set the general_log global variable to on and specify the general_log_file path. After the capture, review the log file and then set the variable to off. A common mistake is leaving it on and producing terabytes of data or masking important alerts under noise. Always plan targeted captures, limit the capture window, and secure the resulting log files for analysis. General Query Log: Forensics with Cost means enable the general query log only for time-limited forensic captures; it is a complete trace but too heavy for continuous production use.. In practical terms, when to enable, what it records, and performance trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › General Query Log
General Query Log
Complete statement capture
Records every statement, connection, and disconnection. Use only as a temporary forensic capture because of its performance and storage cost.
Runtime control
You can enable and disable the general log at runtime for targeted captures, then secure and analyze the log file.
Performance warning
Do not leave the general query log enabled on production servers where latency and disk are concerns.
Example runtime commands
SET GLOBAL general_log = 'ON';
SET GLOBAL general_log_file = '/var/log/mysql/mysql.log';
-- Perform forensic activity
SET GLOBAL general_log = 'OFF';
Enable the log, perform targeted actions or replay suspected malicious steps, then turn it off and collect the file for analysis.
Key takeaway
Plan and limit forensic captures. Secure the generated log files and remove them from high-volume production disks if necessary.

screens.title: Slow Query Log: Performance Signals that Reveal Abuse
screens.narratorSegment: The slow query log captures queries that exceed a configured execution time threshold, set by the long_query_time variable. While it is primarily a tool for performance tuning, it has a security role: sustained or suddenly appearing resource-intensive queries may indicate denial-of-service attempts or data exfiltration activity that scans or extracts large data sets. To use it for security, set long_query_time to a sensible value — for forensic captures you can lower it — enable the slow query log, and then inspect entries for unusual patterns such as many SELECT statements with large result sets or queries that repeatedly use functions to delay execution. A common pitfall is confusing slow queries caused by missing indexes with malicious activity. Always correlate slow-log entries with query origin, user, and time of day before concluding malicious intent. In practice, slow logs complement the error and binary logs; slow logs surface suspicious load, error logs provide server context, and binary logs show the exact data changes. Slow Query Log: Performance Signals that Reveal Abuse means use the slow query log to find resource-intensive queries and investigate whether they stem from malicious activity or performance issues.. In practical terms, detect resource-intensive queries and potential exfiltration attempts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Slow Query Log
Definition
Slow Query Log
Logs queries slower than long_query_time. Useful for tuning and for spotting suspicious, heavy queries used in abuse scenarios.
Config example
slow_query_log = 1, slow_query_log_file = /var/log/mysql/mysql-slow.log, and long_query_time = 1 log queries longer than one second.
Security use
High volume of slow queries by a single user may indicate attempted data extraction or resource abuse.
Concrete example
Lower long_query_time to 0.5 seconds in a controlled window and run SELECT SLEEP to generate a slow-log entry. Then check the slow log for entries listing execution time and query text.
Check your understanding
If a slow query is caused by a missing index, it may look similar to a malicious heavy query. Correlate user, frequency, and intent before escalating.

screens.title: Binary Log (Binlog): Immutable Change History
screens.narratorSegment: The binary log records all statements that change data, including DML and DDL. Its primary uses are replication and point-in-time recovery, but from a security perspective it is extremely valuable because it creates an ordered record of who changed what and when. Unlike general logs, binlogs are compact and designed for efficient storage, and they are typically enabled in production to support recovery and replication. Use the binlog for forensic reconstruction of data integrity incidents: you can replay or inspect events to find the statements that caused unexpected modifications. A frequent misconception is that binlogs always include usernames; depending on how statements are executed, you may need to correlate binlog events with connection logs or audit logs to attribute actions to specific users. Ensure log_bin is enabled in my. cnf and that binlog files are protected and rotated according to your retention policy. In practice, binary logs form the canonical source for reconstructing the sequence of data changes during an investigation. Binary Log (Binlog): Immutable Change History means enable and protect binlogs so you can reconstruct data modifications and support forensic analysis and recovery.. In practical terms, why binlogs are crucial for forensic reconstruction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Binary Log
Definition
Binary Log
Records all data-modifying statements. Used for replication, point-in-time recovery, and forensic reconstruction of changes.
Config example
log_bin=/var/lib/mysql/mysql-bin in my.cnf enables binary logging and defines the file prefix and location.
Security benefit
Provides an ordered, replayable record of data changes that supports investigations into who changed what and when.
Practical note
Binlogs may not directly include user identity for every event. Correlate binlog contents with connection records, general logs when captured, or the Enterprise Audit Log for full attribution.
Key takeaway
Keep binlogs enabled and protected. They are the source of truth for reconstructing data modification events during forensics.

screens.title: MySQL Enterprise Audit Log
screens.narratorSegment: For organizations that need strict compliance, the MySQL Enterprise Audit Log provides a more granular and configurable audit trail than standard logs. The audit plugin can record connections, queries, DDL, DML, and privilege changes, and you can filter events by user, host, or database to reduce noise. Audit output can be written to a file, to syslog, or in structured formats like JSON for ingestion by external systems. The plugin supports rotation settings so you can prevent unbounded file growth. Because audit logs are designed for tamper-resistance and fine-grained filtering, they are often required for regulatory programs. To enable it you install the audit_log plugin and set variables such as audit_log_policy and audit_log_format; you can also rotate by size. A practical point: audit logging carries overhead and requires careful filtering and retention planning. If you rely on it for compliance, ensure the plugin configuration and retention policy meet your regulatory evidence requirements. MySQL Enterprise Audit Log means the enterprise audit log offers configurable, tamper-resistant auditing for compliance, with filters and structured output for ingestion into log systems.. In practical terms, a configurable, tamper-resistant audit trail for compliance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Enterprise Audit Log
Definition
MySQL Enterprise Audit Log
A plugin-based audit solution that records detailed events, supports filtering, and writes structured output suitable for compliance and ingestion.
Enable example
INSTALL PLUGIN audit_log SONAME 'audit_log.so';
SET GLOBAL audit_log_policy = 'ALL';
SET GLOBAL audit_log_format = 'JSON';
SET GLOBAL audit_log_file = '/var/log/mysql/audit.log';
Why choose Enterprise audit
It gives tamper-resistant trails, fine-grained event filtering, and structured formats needed for regulatory evidence and forensic attribution.
Practical caveat
Audit logging requires planning: decide which events you must retain, and configure rotation and secure storage to meet compliance retention windows.

For example, set log_error to a secure path and enable slow query logging with an appropriate threshold for your workload. When deciding what to put in my. cnf, prefer enabling low-overhead logs such as error and binlog by default. Avoid placing the general query log persistently in production. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Configuring Logs
Process
Add persistent settings to my.cnf
Edit the [mysqld] section and add log paths and flags. Restart MySQL to apply the changes permanently.
Example my.cnf snippet
[mysqld]
log_error=/var/log/mysql/error.log
slow_query_log=1
slow_query_log_file=/var/log/mysql/mysql-slow.log
long_query_time=0.5
log_bin=/var/lib/mysql/mysql-bin
Checklist
  • Place settings under [mysqld].
  • Use secure, writable file locations and correct permissions.
  • Restart the server to apply changes.
  • Document changes for incident readiness.
Key takeaway
Make long-term logging choices in my.cnf and verify after restart so audit capability survives reboots and restarts.

screens.title: Runtime Control and Verification
screens.narratorSegment: You can control several logs at runtime without restarting the server, which is useful for targeted forensic captures or quick checks. For example, you can enable the general query log only for the duration of an investigation, or enable the slow query log and lower the threshold to capture suspect activity. After making a runtime change, always verify the variables with SHOW VARIABLES to confirm the change took effect. A typical verification sequence is to run SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'general_log%'; SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'slow_query_log%'; and SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'long_query_time';. If you enabled a capture, run the actions you want to record and then inspect the log files on disk. Remember that runtime changes do not persist across restarts — if you need persistence, write the settings to my. cnf. A common misunderstanding is to assume a successful runtime SET is durable; it is not. Use runtime control for short, secure captures and rely on persistent config for ongoing requirements. Runtime Control and Verification means use set and show variables for on-the-fly captures and verify with show variables before and after to confirm behavior; persist only when needed.. In practical terms, enable and check logs without restarting the server. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Code Walkthrough
Enable, verify, and disable logs at runtime
-- Enable general log temporarily
SET GLOBAL general_log = 'ON';
SET GLOBAL general_log_file = '/var/log/mysql/mysql.log';
-- Verify
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'general_log%';
-- After capture, disable
SET GLOBAL general_log = 'OFF';
Visualize: run the capture, perform the suspect actions, then disable and collect the file for analysis. Always confirm the variables with SHOW VARIABLES before trusting the capture.
Practical tips
  • Limit capture window to reduce noise and performance impact.
  • Secure produced log files immediately after capture.
  • Document why and when captures were taken for audit trails.
Common mistake
Assuming runtime settings persist. If you need persistence, add the settings to my.cnf and restart.

screens.title: Log Rotation and Retention
screens.narratorSegment: Log rotation prevents logs from consuming all available disk space while retention policies ensure you keep evidence for the required period. On Linux, a common tool is logrotate. A sample configuration rotates MySQL logs daily, keeps a set number of rotated files, compresses old logs, and runs postrotate hooks to reload or notify MySQL if needed. For sensitive audit logs you may need longer retention, often driven by compliance rules. Rotation should be combined with secure archival — move rotated logs off the database host to a dedicated log server or object storage and restrict access. Avoid deleting audit logs prematurely. A frequent mistake is rotating logs without preserving a secure copy, which destroys evidence needed for investigations. When designing retention, align with your organization's policy: shorter for transient performance logs, longer for audit logs used for compliance or legal holds. Log Rotation and Retention means use rotation tools to manage disk usage and enforce retention policies that meet compliance requirements while preserving forensic evidence.. In practical terms, keep disk usage in check and meet compliance timelines. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Rotation & Retention
Logrotate Example
A concise logrotate snippet automates rotation, compression, and postrotate reloads if MySQL is running.
/var/log/mysql/*.log {
  daily
  rotate 7
  compress
  delaycompress
  missingok
  notifempty
  create 640 mysql adm
  sharedscripts
  postrotate
    if test -x /usr/bin/mysqladmin && /usr/bin/mysqladmin ping >/dev/null
    then
      /usr/bin/mysqladmin reload >/dev/null 2>&1
    fi
  endscript
}
Rotate by size or time. For audit logs with compliance needs, retain and archive to off-host storage rather than deleting.
Retention guidance
  • Match retention to compliance demands.
  • Archive critical logs off-host and protect access.
  • Ensure rotation scripts do not interrupt logging integrity.
Key takeaway
Automate rotation, then archive and secure rotated logs to maintain evidence while managing storage.

screens.title: Monitoring for Security Events
screens.narratorSegment: Generating logs is not enough — you must actively monitor them. Effective monitoring combines automated parsing to detect known patterns and periodic manual review to find subtle anomalies. Use log management systems or scripts to parse the error log for repeated failed logins, to look for privilege changes like GRANT or REVOKE, and to identify schema changes. Configure alerts for critical events: many failed logins from a single IP, successful logins from unusual locations or times, high-volume DELETE or UPDATE statements by one user, and schema changes that occur outside scheduled maintenance windows. A common trap is 'alert fatigue' from poorly tuned rules. Start with a handful of high-value alerts and tune thresholds to reduce noise. Even with automation, perform scheduled manual reviews to catch patterns automation misses. Finally, integrate MySQL logs into your centralized log platform so they are retained, indexed, and correlated with other system signals during investigations. Monitoring for Security Events means automate parsing and alerting for high-value events and retain manual review for nuanced anomalies; integrate logs into a central platform for correlation.. In practical terms, automated parsing, alerting, and human review. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Monitoring
Automated Parsing
From logs to alerts
Parse logs to detect repeated failures, privilege or schema changes, and high-volume data-modifying activity. Send those findings to an alerting system for rapid response.
High-value alerts
Repeated failed logins from one IP, successful logins at odd hours, GRANT/REVOKE statements, and bursts of DELETE/UPDATE operations.
Avoid alert fatigue
Start small, tune rules, and correlate events across logs to reduce false positives.
Tools & integration
Send logs to a centralized platform that supports searching and correlation. This makes incident triage faster and preserves logs off-host for integrity.
Key takeaway
Monitoring converts raw logs into actionable alerts; tune and correlate to maintain signal quality and reliable incident detection.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Enable Slow Log and Simulate a Slow Query
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough shows how to enable the slow query log, verify settings, simulate a slow query, and confirm the entry appears in the slow log. First, add or confirm slow_query_log, slow_query_log_file, and long_query_time in my. cnf for persistent setup, or enable them at runtime for a temporary test. Restart or set runtime variables as needed and then verify with SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'slow_query_log%'; and SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'long_query_time';. This test proves the slow log captures events and that your rotation and retention rules will preserve the evidence. Finally, remember to reset any lowered thresholds and to disable temporary captures when testing is complete. Step-by-step
Enable slow log, run a slow query, and verify
1. Configure or enable
Ensure slow_query_log and slow_query_log_file are set, and set long_query_time to 0.5 for testing.
-- Verify runtime variables
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'slow_query_log%';

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These three compact concept cards summarize what to remember. First, the error log records server-level events and failed authentication attempts and should be enabled and monitored as a low-cost, early-warning sensor. Second, the binary log is the authoritative record of data changes and is essential for forensic reconstruction and recovery; protect and retain binlogs according to policy. Third, the general query log is a complete activity trace that is too heavy for continuous production use but invaluable as a time-limited forensic capture; use it sparingly. Keep in mind the slow query log provides performance signals that can hint at abuse, and the Enterprise Audit Log offers the structured, tamper-resistant trail often required for compliance. Lastly, rotate and retain logs according to your compliance needs and feed important events into a monitoring platform so they turn into timely alerts. Which log would you check first if you suspect repeated failed logins? The error log is usually where you start.

fullNarratorScript:
Logs are the backbone of database security monitoring. In this lesson you will learn how the MySQL error log, general query log, slow query log, and binary log each provide distinct signals that help you detect failed logins, track suspicious queries, and reconstruct data changes. You will also see when and how to use the MySQL Enterprise Audit Log for compliance-grade, tamper-resistant event tracking. Practical configuration examples show where to set file paths and how to enable logs temporarily for forensic work. We will cover rotation and retention so logs do not exhaust disk space, plus simple monitoring tactics to alert on brute-force attempts, privilege changes, and unusual data-modifying activity. By the end, you will understand how to choose which logs to enable in production, how to collect them safely, and how logs fit into incident response workflows. Think about a time you needed to answer who changed a table and when; the techniques here explain which log will help you and how to preserve that evidence.

By the end of this chapter you will identify and configure the MySQL logs that matter for security, explain how each log supports incident response, and implement basic log management strategies. First, you will learn to find and set the error, general, slow, and binary log file paths and enable them when appropriate. Second, you will know how to use logs during an investigation — for example, enabling the general query log temporarily to capture forensic detail, or using the binary log to reconstruct data-modifying statements. Third, you will understand the benefits of the MySQL Enterprise Audit Log for compliance and how it differs from standard logs. Finally, you will implement rotation and retention rules and design simple monitoring rules to alert on repeated failures or anomalous changes. Each objective includes a practical competency milestone so you can verify your setup and test a scenario. These objectives focus on secure, evidence-preserving logging rather than indiscriminate verbosity.

This second objectives screen maps each competency to a verification step you can run in a lab. You will verify file paths and variables for logs with SHOW VARIABLES and by checking configuration files. You will enable the slow query log and run a deliberate slow query to confirm entries appear in the slow query file. You will enable the general query log only temporarily to capture forensic queries, then disable it to avoid performance impact. You will test binary logging by inspecting binary log file names when log_bin is enabled. For the Enterprise Audit Log, you will install the audit plugin and set a policy that records the events required by your compliance rules. Each step explains why it matters and a small mnemonic to remember the action. These verification exercises ensure you do more than configure logs — you can prove they contain the evidence you need during an investigation.

Think of MySQL logs as complementary security sensors. The error log reveals server-level errors and authentication failures; the slow query log surfaces resource-heavy statements that could indicate abuse; the general query log is a complete but noisy record of client activity useful for short forensic captures; and the binary log provides an immutable record of data changes. Together these logs help you detect attack patterns — repeated failed logins in the error log, sudden schema changes recorded in the binary log, or a flurry of data-modifying statements that might indicate exfiltration. A common misconception is to enable every log permanently. That increases disk usage and can hurt performance, and it creates so much noise that meaningful alerts can be lost. Instead, treat logs as a layered strategy: enable essential, low-cost logs like the error log and binary log in production, use slow logs where resource abuse is a concern, and enable the general query log only temporarily during an investigation. The practical takeaway is to design logging that preserves evidence without overwhelming your system or analysts. Why MySQL Logs are Security Sensors means choose logs by their signal and cost: error and binary logs for continuous coverage; slow logs for resource monitoring; general log only for targeted forensic capture.. In practical terms, understanding the unique signal each log provides. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The error log is the foundational MySQL log for security. It records server startup and shutdown events, warnings, non-fatal errors, fatal errors, and importantly, authentication failures and access denied messages. For security monitoring you use the error log to spot repeated failed logins that may indicate brute-force attempts and to find SSL loading errors which can weaken encrypted connections. The error log path is configured via the log_error variable in my. cnf; a typical setting points to /var/log/mysql/error. log. Regularly review the error log and ensure it is writable only by privileged users to preserve integrity. A common misconception is to treat the error log as proof of every attack; it can miss successful but stealthy data modifications. So use the error log as an early-warning sensor that should feed alerts for further investigation, not as a sole source of truth. Your next steps are to confirm log_error is set and to build alerts for repeated authentication failures. Error Log: The First Line of Defense means use the error log to detect server-level issues and authentication problems; configure secure file paths and alert on repeated failures.. In practical terms, detect server issues, failed logins, and ssl problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The general query log records every statement a client executes along with connection and disconnection events. It is the most detailed trace you can get from MySQL, which makes it extremely valuable for forensic analysis when you need to see exactly what queries a compromised account executed. However, it comes at a heavy cost: high disk usage and significant performance overhead if left on in production. The recommended approach is to enable the general query log only temporarily for debugging or incident response, capture the activity you need, then disable it. For runtime control, you can set the general_log global variable to on and specify the general_log_file path. After the capture, review the log file and then set the variable to off. A common mistake is leaving it on and producing terabytes of data or masking important alerts under noise. Always plan targeted captures, limit the capture window, and secure the resulting log files for analysis. General Query Log: Forensics with Cost means enable the general query log only for time-limited forensic captures; it is a complete trace but too heavy for continuous production use.. In practical terms, when to enable, what it records, and performance trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The slow query log captures queries that exceed a configured execution time threshold, set by the long_query_time variable. While it is primarily a tool for performance tuning, it has a security role: sustained or suddenly appearing resource-intensive queries may indicate denial-of-service attempts or data exfiltration activity that scans or extracts large data sets. To use it for security, set long_query_time to a sensible value — for forensic captures you can lower it — enable the slow query log, and then inspect entries for unusual patterns such as many SELECT statements with large result sets or queries that repeatedly use functions to delay execution. A common pitfall is confusing slow queries caused by missing indexes with malicious activity. Always correlate slow-log entries with query origin, user, and time of day before concluding malicious intent. The binary log records all statements that change data, including DML and DDL. Unlike general logs, binlogs are compact and designed for efficient storage, and they are typically enabled in production to support recovery and replication. Use the binlog for forensic reconstruction of data integrity incidents: you can replay or inspect events to find the statements that caused unexpected modifications. These three compact concept cards summarize what to remember. First, the error log records server-level events and failed authentication attempts and should be enabled and monitored as a low-cost, early-warning sensor. Second, the binary log is the authoritative record of data changes and is essential for forensic reconstruction and recovery; protect and retain binlogs according to policy. Third, the general query log is a complete activity trace that is too heavy for continuous production use but invaluable as a time-limited forensic capture; use it sparingly. Keep in mind the slow query log provides performance signals that can hint at abuse, and the Enterprise Audit Log offers the structured, tamper-resistant trail often required for compliance. Lastly, rotate and retain logs according to your compliance needs and feed important events into a monitoring platform so they turn into timely alerts. Which log would you check first if you suspect repeated failed logins? The error log is usually where you start.

Remember log_error for the error log file path, general_log and general_log_file for ad-hoc full captures, slow_query_log with slow_query_log_file and long_query_time for performance signals, and log_bin to enable the binary log. For high-grade auditing, the audit_log plugin and variables such as audit_log_policy and audit_log_format let you tailor what to record and how to output it. When building processes, always include rotation and retention to keep logs manageable and preserved for compliance.
